title: Cloudflare: Too Many Redirects Error when Proxying
description: Troubleshooting SSL/TLS encryption modes and flexible proxy settings causing infinite redirect loops.
content: When proxying web traffic through Cloudflare for a client application, I ran into the infamous `ERR_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS` browser error. The web server was running Nginx with an SSL certificate issued via Let's Encrypt, yet any HTTPS request triggered an infinite redirect loop.
### Understanding the Root Cause

The issue stemmed from a mismatch between Cloudflare's SSL/TLS encryption mode and the backend server configuration. Cloudflare was set to **Flexible SSL mode**. In Flexible mode, Cloudflare connects to the origin server over unencrypted HTTP (port 80).

However, our Nginx configuration had a strict rule redirecting all HTTP traffic to HTTPS (`return 301 https://$host$request_uri;`). This created a classic infinite loop:
1. Visitor requests HTTPS page.
2. Cloudflare receives HTTPS request, offloads SSL, and forwards request to origin over HTTP.
3. Nginx sees HTTP request and responds with a 301 Redirect to HTTPS.
4. Cloudflare receives the 301 and sends it back to the browser.
5. Browser repeats step 1 endlessly.
### The Solution

To resolve this, I updated the Cloudflare SSL/TLS setting from **Flexible** to **Full (Strict)**. This instructs Cloudflare to establish an encrypted HTTPS connection to the origin server using valid SSL certificates.

Additionally, I verified Nginx headers to ensure `X-Forwarded-Proto` was correctly set:
```nginx
proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
```
### Key Takeaways
Always align your CDN proxy SSL mode with your origin server's HTTPS enforcement policies. Using Full (Strict) mode ensures end-to-end security while avoiding redirection loops.

title: Up and Running with AWS EC2
description: Setting up elastic compute cloud instances, security groups, and automated deployment pipelines.
content: Deploying scalable cloud compute instances is a fundamental milestone in full-stack web engineering. Recently, I set up a dedicated AWS EC2 architecture for hosting containerized Node.js applications.
### Instance Provisioning & Security Groups

I selected an Ubuntu Server 22.04 LTS t3.micro instance within an AWS Free Tier allocation. Designing proper Security Group rules was critical:
- **SSH (Port 22)**: Restricted strictly to static administrator IP ranges.
- **HTTP (Port 80) & HTTPS (Port 443)**: Open to public web traffic (`0.0.0.0/0`).
### System Initialization & Deployment

After connecting via SSH using RSA key pairs, I configured Docker and Docker Compose to manage process isolation. Setting up systemd services ensured automatic service recovery on reboot:
```bash
sudo systemctl enable docker
sudo systemctl start docker
```
### Key Takeaways
Never expose SSH ports globally. Always implement principle of least privilege in AWS Security Groups and rely on automated systemd daemons for uptime reliability.

title: Up and Running with AWS VPC
description: Configuring custom virtual private clouds, subnets, route tables, and NAT gateways.
content: Building production cloud infrastructure requires a solid networking foundation. I designed a custom AWS Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) with isolated public and private subnets.
### Network Architecture Design

- **CIDR Block**: `10.0.0.0/16` providing 65,536 IP addresses across multi-AZ deployment.
- **Public Subnets**: `10.0.1.0/24` (AZ-a) & `10.0.2.0/24` (AZ-b) for Internet Gateway (IGW) route attachment.
- **Private Subnets**: `10.0.10.0/24` & `10.0.20.0/24` hosting backend application services and databases isolated from direct internet access.
### Route Tables & NAT Gateway

To allow backend private servers to fetch security patches without exposing open inbound ports, I attached a NAT Gateway inside the public subnet and pointed the private route table default route (`0.0.0.0/0`) to the NAT Gateway target.
### Key Takeaways
Separating public web nodes from private database networks dramatically reduces attack surface while maintaining patch automation.

title: Dynamically Load Ansible Inventory with EC2 IP
description: Automating dynamic server inventory discovery for configuration management across cloud environments.
content: Manually updating static Ansible inventory files whenever AWS EC2 instances scale or restart with new IP addresses is error-prone. To solve this, I integrated the `amazon.aws.aws_ec2` inventory plugin.
### Dynamic Plugin Configuration

Creating `aws_ec2.yaml` enabled automated discovery based on AWS resource tags:
```yaml
plugin: amazon.aws.aws_ec2
regions:
  - ap-southeast-1
keyed_groups:
  - key: tags.Environment
    prefix: env
  - key: tags.Role
    prefix: role
```
### Execution & Verification
Running `ansible-inventory -i aws_ec2.yaml --graph` dynamically structured hosts into dynamic groups (`env_production`, `role_webserver`), eliminating hardcoded IPs from Playbooks.
### Key Takeaways
Infrastructure automation thrives on metadata and tags. Dynamic inventory plugins save hours of manual maintenance during deployments.

title: Generate Terraform from existing AWS infrastructure
description: Importing legacy cloud resources into infrastructure-as-code state files seamlessly.
content: When taking over cloud environments initially created via the AWS Management Console, transitioning them to Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform is essential for reliability.
### The Import Workflow

Using Terraform 1.5+ declarative `import` blocks allowed clean resource mapping:
```hcl
import {
  to = aws_s3_bucket.portfolio_assets
  id = "my-portfolio-assets-bucket"
}
```
Running `terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated_resources.tf` automatically generated HCL configurations, which I then refactored into modular code structures.
### Key Takeaways
Imperative manual changes are technical debt. Importing legacy infrastructure into version-controlled Terraform code guarantees repeatable, disaster-recoverable environments.

title: My First Commit
description: This is my first commit to my portfolio website. Excited to share my software engineering journey.
content: Today marks an exciting milestone: initiating the codebase for my personal portfolio application! As a developer passionate about intuitive user experiences and clean code, building a tailored digital workspace has been high on my list.
### Tech Stack Selection

I chose a modern, high-performance web frontend stack:
- **Vite & React 19**: Ultra-fast module reloading and component architecture.
- **TypeScript**: Strict type safety across components and asset schemas.
- **Tailwind CSS v4 & DaisyUI 5**: CSS-first custom design system with rich dark and light themes.
### Architectural Goals
My goal is to keep the portfolio fast, accessible, minimalist, and responsive across device screens—serving as a live catalog of projects, technical skills, education, and development journals.
### Looking Ahead
This is just the beginning. I'll continue documenting technical learnings, architectural breakdowns, and real-world project achievements right here in my programming journal.
